questions.question: In procedural programming, a program is broken down into reusable, callable blocks of code. Which of the following terms are all used (across various languages) to refer to these blocks?

choices.statement: Objects, classes, and interfaces
Procedures, routines, subroutines, methods, and functions
Facts, rules, and predicates
Threads, processes, and handlers

questions.hint: Different languages use different names for the same reusable idea.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a compiler and an interpreter when processing a procedural language like C?

choices.statement: A compiler translates the entire source code into machine code before execution, while an interpreter executes code line-by-line at runtime
A compiler only works with object-oriented languages, while an interpreter only works with procedural languages
A compiler and an interpreter perform the exact same function with no meaningful difference
An interpreter produces a standalone executable file, while a compiler does not

questions.hint: One translates everything before the program runs; the other translates as it goes.

questions.question: The C programming language was developed in the early 1970s at Bell Labs, largely to support the development of which operating system?

choices.statement: Windows
macOS
MS-DOS
Unix

questions.hint: Think of the famous operating system that came out of Bell Labs.

questions.question: Why do C programmers commonly split a large program's source code into multiple files (e.g., separate .c and header .h files)?

choices.statement: To allow different files to be compiled independently, improving compilation efficiency and organization
To make the program run using an interpreter instead of a compiler
Because C does not allow more than one function per file
To automatically convert the program into an object-oriented structure

questions.hint: Think about compiling pieces separately and keeping a large program organized.

choices.statement: float
char
int
double

questions.hint: All five variables hold whole numbers.

questions.question: What is the difference between a variable declaration and a variable definition in C, and what role does the extern keyword play?

choices.statement: A declaration allocates memory and assigns a value; a definition only announces the variable's type; extern deletes a variable

A declaration tells the compiler a variable's type and name without necessarily allocating memory; a definition actually allocates storage; extern is used to declare a variable that is defined in another file
There is no difference between declaration and definition in C; extern is only used for functions, never variables
A definition can only occur inside main(), while a declaration can occur anywhere

questions.hint: One announces a variable's type and name; the other actually reserves storage.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes pointers and the address-of operator (&) in C?

choices.statement: The & operator dereferences a pointer to retrieve the value it points to
Pointers are exclusive to C and are not related to memory addresses at all
Pointers in C cannot be null and must always point to valid memory
The & operator retrieves the memory address of a variable, and a pointer is declared using * to store such an address

questions.hint: One symbol gives you an address; the other is used when declaring a variable that stores one.

questions.question: In the Fibonacci program, the variable c is declared inside main() and used only within the for loop. If another c were declared as a global variable outside main(), what would happen inside the function?

choices.statement: The program would fail to compile due to a naming conflict
The global c would automatically overwrite the local c's value permanently
The local c would take precedence (shadow) the global c within the scope of main()
C does not allow both local and global variables to share the same name under any circumstance

questions.hint: When two variables share a name, the one declared closer to the code wins.

questions.question: C primarily passes arguments to functions using call-by-value. How can a C function still modify a caller's original variable, effectively simulating call-by-reference?

choices.statement: By passing a pointer to the variable, allowing the function to dereference and modify the original memory location
By declaring the function as static
By using the extern keyword in the function header
C has no way to modify a caller's variable from within a function

questions.hint: Give the function the address of the variable instead of a copy of its value.

questions.question: The Fibonacci program shown uses an iterative (for loop) approach. If this were rewritten as a recursive function instead, what is a key consideration unique to recursion that iteration does not have?

choices.statement: Recursive functions cannot return a value
Each recursive call adds a new frame to the call stack, so deep or unterminated recursion can cause a stack overflow
Recursive functions must always be declared using the void return type
Recursion eliminates the need for a base case or terminating condition

questions.hint: Every call needs its own space in memory, and that space is limited.
Check which value goes into a and which into b when the function is called.
